content: Hearing, also known as audition, is one of the five traditional senses and refers to the ability to detect sound. In humans and other vertebrates, hearing is primarily facilitated by the auditory system. Sound waves are detected by the ear and converted into nerve impulses, which are then interpreted by the brain. Similar to the sense of touch, hearing relies on the organism's sensitivity to the movement of molecules in the external environment. Both hearing and touch are classified as mechanosensory processes. Hearing in Animals Not all sounds are audible to all animals. Each species has a specific range of hearing, defined by both loudness (amplitude) and pitch (frequency). Many animals rely on sound for communication, and in these species, hearing is critical for survival and reproduction. For species that use sound as a primary mode of communication, their hearing is often most sensitive to the range of pitches used in their calls or vocalizations. Sounds within the human-audible range are referred to as audio or sonic. Frequencies above this range are termed ultrasonic, while those below are called infrasonic. For example, bats use ultrasound for echolocation during flight, and dogs can hear ultrasonic frequencies, which is the principle behind silent dog whistles. Snakes detect infrasound through their bodies, while whales, giraffes, and elephants use infrasound for communication. Despite significant advances, the molecular mechanisms of sound transduction in the cochlea and the brain's auditory processing remain incompletely understood. Hearing in Humans Humans can typically hear sounds with frequencies ranging from 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Human hearing is capable of distinguishing subtle differences in loudness (intensity) and pitch (frequency) across this wide range. However, the range of frequency detection varies significantly with age, occupational noise exposure, and gender. Some individuals can hear pitches as high as 22 kHz or beyond, while others may be limited to around 16 kHz. Most adults experience a decline in their ability to hear frequencies above 8 kHz starting in early middle age. Mechanism of Hearing Hearing in humans involves a complex process where sound waves are transformed into nerve impulses. Outer Ear The visible part of the outer ear is called the auricle or pinna. This convoluted structure arises from the opening of the ear canal on either side of the head. The auricle helps direct sound waves into the ear canal. Both the auricle and the ear canal amplify and guide sound waves toward the tympanic membrane (eardrum). The shape and length of the human external ear preferentially amplify sounds in the speech frequency range, improving the signal-to-noise ratio for speech sounds. Middle Ear The eardrum is stretched across the front of a bony, air-filled cavity known as the middle ear. The tympanic membrane functions like the head of a drum, while the middle ear cavity acts as the drum's body. The middle ear's primary role in hearing is to convert sound waves in the air into fluid vibrations within the cochlea of the inner ear. Sound waves move the tympanic membrane, which in turn moves the ossicles (small bones in the middle ear), ultimately transmitting vibrations to the cochlear fluid. Inner Ear The cochlea is a snail-shaped, fluid-filled chamber divided along its length by a membranous partition. It propagates mechanical signals from the middle ear as waves in its fluid and membranes, converting them into nerve impulses that are transmitted to the brain. The cochlea is also responsible for sensations of balance and motion. Central Auditory System Sound information, encoded as electrical impulses (spikes) in the auditory nerve fibers, travels through the cochlear nuclei to the superior olivary complex in the brainstem. From there, it passes via the lateral lemniscus to the inferior colliculus in the midbrain, undergoing further processing at each stage. The information eventually reaches the medial geniculate body in the thalamus, which relays it to the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe of the brain. The primary auditory cortex connects to other cortical regions involved in identifying and localizing sound sources, as well as perceiving speech, music, and language. These association areas also receive input from the visual cortex and other sensory regions. Representation of Loudness, Pitch, and Timbre Auditory nerve fibers transmit information through discrete electrical impulses known as action potentials. As the loudness of a sound increases, the rate of action potentials in the auditory nerve fibers also increases. Conversely, at lower sound intensities, the rate of action potentials decreases. Different frequencies (pitch) and sound qualities (timbre) are represented in the auditory nerve through a combination of rate-place coding and temporal fine-structure coding. For example, different frequencies elicit maximum responses at specific locations along the organ of Corti, while low-pitched sounds (below approximately 1500 Hz) are represented by the repetition of neural firing patterns (volley coding). Loudness and sound duration can also influence pitch perception to a small extent. For sounds above 4000 Hz, an increase in loudness may slightly raise the perceived pitch. Localization of Sound Humans can typically hear a wide range of sound frequencies, from about 20 Hz to 20 kHz. The ability to determine the location of a sound source, known as sound localization, depends on the hearing ability of both ears and the specific characteristics of the sound. Since each ear is positioned on opposite sides of the head, a sound will reach the closer ear first and with greater amplitude. The shape of the pinna (outer ear) and the head itself cause frequency-dependent variations in sound attenuation as it travels from the source to the ear. These variations depend on both the azimuthal angle and the elevation of the sound source and are described by the head-related transfer function (HRTF). As a result, humans can localize sound in both azimuth and altitude. The brain's ability to localize sound relies on interaural intensity differences and interaural temporal or phase differences. Additionally, humans can estimate the distance of a sound source based on environmental reflections, such as room reverberation. Some blind individuals use human echolocation, emitting clicks or taps and interpreting the resulting echoes to navigate their surroundings. Hearing and Language Humans develop spoken language within the first few years of life, and hearing impairment can hinder not only the ability to speak but also the ability to understand spoken language. If a child with severe hearing impairment is not identified early, communication difficulties may already have caused social and familial challenges. However, children who are part of a Deaf community, where sign language is used, may not face the same barriers. In many developed countries, newborn hearing screening is conducted to prevent the inadvertent isolation of a deaf child in a hearing family. While sign language is a complete form of communication, literacy often depends on understanding spoken language. Written language in most cases encodes the sound of words in symbols. Individuals who hear and learn to speak and read retain the ability to read even if their hearing becomes impaired later in life. However, those who never heard well enough to learn spoken language rarely achieve proficient reading skills. Early identification of hearing impairment is crucial for children with significant hearing loss to develop spoken language. Listening also plays a vital role in learning a second language. Hearing Tests Hearing can be assessed through behavioral tests using an audiometer. Electrophysiological tests, such as auditory brainstem evoked potentials (ABR), otoacoustic emissions, and electrocochleography (EchoG), provide accurate measurements of hearing thresholds, even in unconscious individuals. Advances in these techniques have made infant hearing screening widespread. Hearing Underwater Hearing thresholds and the ability to localize sound sources are reduced underwater, where the speed of sound is faster than in air. Underwater hearing occurs primarily through bone conduction, and sound localization depends on differences in amplitude detected via bone conduction.
